A map with 1,600 small deforestation polygons is hard to read. **Kernel density** spreads each polygon
over a neighborhood and adds everything into a continuous surface: the result is a **heat map** that
shows where deforestation is concentrated.

The script I used computed two densities, one weighted by polygon **area** and one by **count** only,
normalized each between 0 and 1 and took the average. That way, both one large clearing and many small
ones show up as "hot". Then it computed the mean index inside each protected area.

![PRODES 2025 deforestation density index (average of the area and count densities, from 0 to 1).](../imagens/artigos/kernel.png){fig-alt="Heat map over the Novo Progresso region, from light yellow to red. Most of the heat lies outside the protected areas, in a band east of Jamanxim National Forest. The hottest point, marked with an X, lies on the border between the Tapajós Environmental Protection Area and Jamanxim National Forest, to the west. Protected area boundaries are drawn in black."}

## How it works

```{mermaid}
%%| eval: true
%%| fig-cap: "From polygon to index by protected area"
flowchart LR
    A["PRODES 2025<br/>polygons"] --> B["Point inside<br/>each polygon"]
    B --> C["Kernel weighted<br/>by area"]
    B --> D["Unweighted kernel<br/>(count)"]
    C --> E["Normalize<br/>0 to 1"]
    D --> F["Normalize<br/>0 to 1"]
    E --> G["Average"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["Mean by<br/>protected area"]
```

- **Search radius:** how far each point "spreads" its influence. Here, **10 km**.
- **Cell size:** the resolution of the map. Here, **1 km**.
- **Quartic kernel:** the weight falls smoothly from the center (maximum weight) to the edge of the
  radius (zero). It is the default in ArcGIS and QGIS.
- **Study area:** we only downloaded deforestation inside a rectangle. Outside it, the density would be
  zero without really being zero, so the map and the means by protected area stay **inside the study
  area**.
- **Normalize:** `(value − minimum) / (maximum − minimum)`. Each program computes density on a different
  scale, but after normalizing the results are comparable.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Work in meters
The old script used a radius of `0.777` and a cell of `0.0015`, in **degrees**. A degree of longitude is
about 111 km at the Equator and less further south, so the search "circle" becomes an ellipse. Reproject
to a projection in meters (here, EPSG:5880) and write radius and cell size in meters.
:::

## The code

Data: layers `prodes_amz` (year 2025) and `ucs` of the articles' GeoPackage
([how to download](about.qmd#data)). Names in Portuguese: `pontos` = points, `peso` = weight,
`recorte` = study area, `indice` = index, `kd_qtde` = count density, `RAIO` = radius, `CEL` = cell.

::: {.panel-tabset group="programa"}

## ArcGIS Pro

Requires the **Spatial Analyst** extension.

```python
import arcpy
from arcpy.sa import KernelDensity

arcpy.CheckOutExtension("Spatial")
arcpy.env.overwriteOutput = True
arcpy.env.outputCoordinateSystem = arcpy.SpatialReference(5880)   # meters
gpkg = r"C:\dados\artigos.gpkg"
gdb = r"C:\dados\resultados.gdb"

# Downloaded area (the study area): the map and the means stay inside it
recorte = arcpy.Extent(-56.5, -8.5, -54.5, -5.5, spatial_reference=arcpy.SpatialReference(4674))
arcpy.env.extent = recorte.projectAs(arcpy.SpatialReference(5880))

# 1. 2025 polygons, area in hectares and a point inside each one
prodes = arcpy.analysis.Select(gpkg + r"\main.prodes_amz", r"memory\prodes",
                               "year = 2025 AND UPPER(main_class) = 'DESMATAMENTO'")
arcpy.management.RepairGeometry(prodes)
arcpy.management.CalculateGeometryAttributes(
    prodes, [["area_ha", "AREA_GEODESIC"]], area_unit="HECTARES")
pontos = arcpy.management.FeatureToPoint(prodes, r"memory\pontos", "INSIDE")

# 2. Two densities: weighted by area and unweighted (1 km cell, 10 km radius)
kd_area = KernelDensity(pontos, "area_ha", 1000, 10000, "SQUARE_KILOMETERS")
kd_qtde = KernelDensity(pontos, "NONE", 1000, 10000, "SQUARE_KILOMETERS")

# 3. Normalize each one between 0 and 1 and take the average
def normalizar(r):
    arcpy.management.CalculateStatistics(r)
    return (r - r.minimum) / (r.maximum - r.minimum)

indice = (normalizar(kd_area) + normalizar(kd_qtde)) / 2
indice.save(gdb + r"\kernel_indice")

# 4. Mean and maximum of the index in each protected area, only inside the study area
ucs = arcpy.analysis.Select(gpkg + r"\main.ucs", r"memory\ucs", "regiao = 'Amazonia'")
ucs = arcpy.analysis.Clip(ucs, recorte.polygon, r"memory\ucs_recorte")
arcpy.sa.ZonalStatisticsAsTable(ucs, "nome_uc", indice, gdb + r"\kernel_por_uc",
                                "DATA", "MEAN_STD")
```

::: {.callout-note}
The original script normalized with `ZonalStatistics` (minimum and maximum per zone). With a single
zone, the raster's `r.minimum` and `r.maximum` give the same result in one line.
:::

## QGIS

```python
import processing
G = "C:/dados/artigos.gpkg"
SAIDA = "C:/dados/"

def rodar(alg, **p):
    p.setdefault("OUTPUT", "memory:")
    return processing.run(alg, p)["OUTPUT"]

# 1. 2025 polygons, area in hectares and a point inside each one (in meters)
prodes = rodar("native:extractbyexpression", INPUT=f"{G}|layername=prodes_amz",
               EXPRESSION="year = 2025 AND upper(main_class) = 'DESMATAMENTO'")
prodes = rodar("native:fixgeometries", INPUT=prodes)
prodes = rodar("native:removenullgeometries", INPUT=prodes, REMOVE_EMPTY=True)  # slivers
prodes = rodar("native:fieldcalculator", INPUT=prodes, FIELD_NAME="area_ha", FIELD_TYPE=0,
               FIELD_PRECISION=4,
               FORMULA="area(transform($geometry, 'EPSG:4674', 'ESRI:102033')) / 10000")
pontos = rodar("native:pointonsurface", INPUT=prodes)
pontos = rodar("native:reprojectlayer", INPUT=pontos, TARGET_CRS="EPSG:5880")

# 2. Heat map (quartic kernel), weighted and unweighted
kernel = dict(INPUT=pontos, RADIUS=10000, PIXEL_SIZE=1000, KERNEL=0, OUTPUT_VALUE=0)
kd_area = rodar("native:heatmapkerneldensityestimation", **kernel, WEIGHT_FIELD="area_ha",
                OUTPUT=SAIDA + "kd_area.tif")
kd_qtde = rodar("native:heatmapkerneldensityestimation", **kernel,
                OUTPUT=SAIDA + "kd_qtde.tif")

# 3. Normalize (0 to 1) and take the average
norm_area = rodar("native:rescaleraster", INPUT=kd_area, BAND=1, MINIMUM=0, MAXIMUM=1,
                  OUTPUT=SAIDA + "kd_area_norm.tif")
norm_qtde = rodar("native:rescaleraster", INPUT=kd_qtde, BAND=1, MINIMUM=0, MAXIMUM=1,
                  OUTPUT=SAIDA + "kd_qtde_norm.tif")
indice = rodar("gdal:rastercalculator", INPUT_A=norm_area, BAND_A=1, INPUT_B=norm_qtde,
               BAND_B=1, FORMULA="(A + B) / 2", RTYPE=5, OUTPUT=SAIDA + "kernel_media.tif")

# The heat map only covers the points' extent plus the radius, and writes "no data" where the
# density is zero: extend it to the study area and replace "no data" with zero
indice = rodar("gdal:warpreproject", INPUT=indice, TARGET_CRS="EPSG:5880",
               TARGET_RESOLUTION=1000, TARGET_EXTENT="-56.5,-54.5,-8.5,-5.5",
               TARGET_EXTENT_CRS="EPSG:4674", OUTPUT=SAIDA + "kernel_recorte.tif")
indice = rodar("native:fillnodata", INPUT=indice, BAND=1, FILL_VALUE=0,
               OUTPUT=SAIDA + "kernel_indice.tif")

# 4. Mean and maximum of the index in each protected area, only inside the study area
ucs = rodar("native:extractbyexpression", INPUT=f"{G}|layername=ucs",
            EXPRESSION="regiao = 'Amazonia'")
ucs = rodar("native:extractbyextent", INPUT=ucs, CLIP=True,
            EXTENT="-56.5,-54.5,-8.5,-5.5 [EPSG:4674]")
ucs = rodar("native:fixgeometries", INPUT=ucs)
ucs = rodar("native:reprojectlayer", INPUT=ucs, TARGET_CRS="EPSG:5880")
por_uc = rodar("native:zonalstatisticsfb", INPUT=ucs, INPUT_RASTER=indice, RASTER_BAND=1,
               STATISTICS=[2, 6], COLUMN_PREFIX="idx_")          # 2 = mean, 6 = maximum
for f in por_uc.getFeatures():
    print(f["nome_uc"], round(f["idx_mean"], 3), round(f["idx_max"], 3))
QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer(QgsRasterLayer(indice, "Kernel index"))
```

**Heatmap** is under Processing → Interpolation (in QGIS 3, the ID is
`qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation`). From the menus, step 3 is **Rescale raster** twice and a
**Raster calculator** with `("norm_area@1" + "norm_qtde@1") / 2`.

## PostGIS

PostGIS computes a kernel without rasters: a **grid of points** every 1 km and, for each grid point, the
sum of the quartic weights of the deforestation within 10 km.

```sql
-- 1. A point inside each 2025 polygon (in meters) and the area in hectares
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS artigos.kernel_pontos;
CREATE TABLE artigos.kernel_pontos AS
SELECT ST_Transform(ST_PointOnSurface(g), 5880) AS geom,
       ST_Area(g::geography) / 10000 AS area_ha
FROM (SELECT ST_CollectionExtract(ST_MakeValid(geom), 3) AS g
      FROM artigos.prodes_amz
      WHERE year = 2025 AND upper(main_class) = 'DESMATAMENTO') p
WHERE NOT ST_IsEmpty(g);
CREATE INDEX ON artigos.kernel_pontos USING gist (geom);

-- 2. 1 km grid over the points' extent (plus a 10 km margin) and the two densities
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS artigos.kernel_grade;
CREATE TABLE artigos.kernel_grade AS
WITH grade AS (
    SELECT ST_Centroid(c.geom) AS geom
    FROM ST_SquareGrid(1000, (SELECT ST_SetSRID(ST_Expand(ST_Extent(geom), 10000)::geometry, 5880)
                              FROM artigos.kernel_pontos)) AS c
),
quartico AS (                       -- weight: (1 - (d/r)²)², from 1 at the center to 0 at 10 km
    SELECT g.geom, p.area_ha,
           power(1 - power(ST_Distance(g.geom, p.geom) / 10000, 2), 2) AS w
    FROM grade g
    JOIN artigos.kernel_pontos p ON ST_DWithin(g.geom, p.geom, 10000)
)
SELECT geom, sum(w * area_ha) AS kd_area, sum(w) AS kd_qtde
FROM quartico
GROUP BY geom;

-- 3. Normalize and average (cells with no deforestation nearby stay at 0)
ALTER TABLE artigos.kernel_grade ADD COLUMN indice numeric;
WITH lim AS (SELECT max(kd_area) AS ma, max(kd_qtde) AS mq FROM artigos.kernel_grade)
UPDATE artigos.kernel_grade SET indice = ((kd_area / ma) + (kd_qtde / mq)) / 2 FROM lim;
CREATE INDEX ON artigos.kernel_grade USING gist (geom);

-- 4. Mean and maximum of the index in each protected area, only inside the study area
--    (cells with zero count)
WITH ucs AS (
    SELECT nome_uc,
           ST_Transform(ST_Intersection(geom, ST_MakeEnvelope(-56.5, -8.5, -54.5, -5.5, 4674)),
                        5880) AS geom
    FROM artigos.ucs
    WHERE regiao = 'Amazonia'
)
SELECT u.nome_uc,
       round(avg(coalesce(k.indice, 0)), 3) AS idx_media,
       round(max(coalesce(k.indice, 0)), 3) AS idx_max
FROM ucs u
CROSS JOIN LATERAL ST_SquareGrid(1000, u.geom) AS c
LEFT JOIN artigos.kernel_grade k ON k.geom = ST_Centroid(c.geom)
WHERE ST_Intersects(ST_Centroid(c.geom), u.geom)
GROUP BY u.nome_uc
ORDER BY idx_media DESC;
```

The minimum of each density is zero (far from any deforestation), so normalization becomes just
`value / maximum`.

## Python

```python
import numpy as np
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import box
from rasterio.transform import from_origin
from rasterstats import zonal_stats

G = "dados/artigos.gpkg"
RAIO, CEL = 10_000, 1_000                         # meters
recorte = gpd.GeoSeries([box(-56.5, -8.5, -54.5, -5.5)], crs=4674)

# 1. 2025 polygons, area in hectares and a point inside each one (in meters)
prodes = gpd.read_file(G, layer="prodes_amz")
prodes = prodes[(prodes["year"] == 2025) & (prodes["main_class"].str.upper() == "DESMATAMENTO")]
prodes["geometry"] = prodes.make_valid(method="structure", keep_collapsed=False)
prodes = prodes[~prodes.is_empty]
peso = prodes.to_crs("ESRI:102033").area.values / 10_000
pontos = prodes.representative_point().to_crs(5880)
x, y = pontos.x.values, pontos.y.values

# 2. 1 km grid over the study area and quartic kernel, point by point
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = recorte.to_crs(5880).total_bounds
x0, y1 = xmin, ymax
ncol = int((xmax - x0) // CEL) + 1
nlin = int((y1 - ymin) // CEL) + 1
cx = x0 + (np.arange(ncol) + 0.5) * CEL           # column centers
cy = y1 - (np.arange(nlin) + 0.5) * CEL           # row centers
kd_area = np.zeros((nlin, ncol))
kd_qtde = np.zeros((nlin, ncol))
for xi, yi, wi in zip(x, y, peso):
    c = slice(max(0, int((xi - RAIO - x0) // CEL)), int((xi + RAIO - x0) // CEL) + 1)
    l = slice(max(0, int((y1 - yi - RAIO) // CEL)), int((y1 - yi + RAIO) // CEL) + 1)
    d2 = (cx[c][None, :] - xi) ** 2 + (cy[l][:, None] - yi) ** 2
    k = np.where(d2 < RAIO ** 2, (1 - d2 / RAIO ** 2) ** 2, 0)
    kd_area[l, c] += wi * k
    kd_qtde[l, c] += k

# 3. Normalize (the minimum is zero) and take the average
indice = (kd_area / kd_area.max() + kd_qtde / kd_qtde.max()) / 2

# 4. Mean and maximum of the index in each protected area, only inside the study area
ucs = gpd.read_file(G, layer="ucs").query("regiao == 'Amazonia'")
ucs = gpd.clip(ucs, recorte).to_crs(5880)
stats = zonal_stats(ucs, indice, affine=from_origin(x0, y1, CEL, CEL),
                    stats=["mean", "max"], nodata=-1)
ucs["idx_media"] = [round(s["mean"], 3) for s in stats]
ucs["idx_max"] = [round(s["max"], 3) for s in stats]
print(ucs[["nome_uc", "idx_media", "idx_max"]].sort_values("idx_media", ascending=False))
np.save("dados/kernel_indice.npy", indice)
```

:::

## Checking the result

The three tested versions gave the same means by protected area (differences up to 0.001). The maximum
varies a little more (up to 0.02), because each program aligns the cell grid differently:

| Protected area (part inside the study area) | Mean index | Maximum (QGIS / PostGIS / Python) |
|---|---:|---|
| Jamanxim National Forest | 0.014 | 0.36 / 0.37 / 0.37 |
| Tapajós Environmental Protection Area | 0.013–0.014 | 0.49 / 0.47 / 0.47 |
| Altamira National Forest | 0.008 | 0.19 / 0.18 / 0.19 |
| Iriri State Forest | 0.005–0.006 | 0.06 / 0.06 / 0.06 |
| Rio Novo National Park | 0.002 | 0.03 / 0.03 / 0.03 |
| Jamanxim National Park | 0.001 | 0.09 / 0.08 / 0.08 |
| Itaituba I National Forest | 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |

: PRODES 2025 kernel density index (0 = no deforestation within 10 km; 1 = the hottest point in the study area). {.striped}

The means are low because the protected areas are huge and most of each one is far from any
deforestation. The **maximum** says more: the Tapajós Environmental Protection Area and Jamanxim National
Forest have points with almost half the intensity of the hottest point in the study area. That point
(the X on the map) lies **outside** the protected areas, on the border between the Tapajós
Environmental Protection Area and Jamanxim National Forest, and most of the heat is in a band east of
Jamanxim National Forest, also outside the protected areas.

## Choosing the radius

The radius changes everything. With 2 km, each clearing becomes an isolated spot; with 50 km, the whole
map turns lukewarm. There is no "right" radius: choose it by the scale of the decision (the working
range of a field team, for example) and **write the value in the legend**. The article
[Prioritizing alerts in ArcGIS Pro and QGIS](12-prioritization-arcgis-qgis.qmd) shows another way to
look at concentration, by grouping nearby polygons.
